name: Phase Five: Scale What Works
title: Phase Five: Scale What Works
answer: Phase Five of the pilot process is about scaling a tool that has already passed its first test, but doing so gradually rather than all at once. It matters because results from a wider group of teachers and students are more trustworthy than results from a few volunteers, and because scaling without training, cost tracking and communication with families tends to leave a tool in the hands of the same few enthusiasts.

sections.body: This idea is the final phase of a pilot, measure, scale sequence, and it covers what happens after a tool has succeeded in its first trial. Rather than rolling the tool out everywhere immediately, the school runs a wider pilot in more classrooms or a second school using the same measure, so that the results can be checked against a broader set of teachers and students. The problem it solves is that early success often comes from a small group of keen volunteers, and that success may not survive contact with ordinary conditions. Scaling also brings its own tasks, such as tracking return on investment, planning training and support, and reporting results back to families. Without these steps, a promising tool can stall or quietly fade away.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, a school that has finished its first pilot repeats the trial on a larger scale, keeping the same measure so the two rounds can be compared. Alongside this, someone keeps a simple spreadsheet of the tool's cost, the training time it requires and the measured benefit, whether that is hours saved or a change in scores, and divides cost by benefit to produce a figure the board can compare across tools. If that figure moves in the wrong direction, the tool returns to review. Training and support are planned at this stage, with the original pilot teachers protected in a coaching role for colleagues who join later. A short summary of what was tested, what happened and what the district decided goes to families, which both shows care in decision making and invites questions that improve the next pilot. The text does not give separate guidance by grade band.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure or formal evidence label for this idea. Its claims rest on practice and reasoning rather than research, for example the observation that results holding up across different teachers and students are more trustworthy than results from three enthusiastic volunteers, and that a tool scaled without support often ends up used by the same few enthusiasts and nobody else. The return on investment method described is a simple spreadsheet comparing cost against measured benefit, not a research finding. Districts that share results openly are said to face less suspicion when they propose something new, which is presented as experience rather than tested evidence.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets several limits on scaling. Growth should not happen all at once, and a tool should only reach every classroom after a wider pilot with the same measure has held up. Cost and benefit must be tracked, and when the ratio drifts in the wrong direction the tool goes back under review rather than continuing by default. Training and support are treated as necessary, because teachers who join after the pilot did not help shape the tool and may not use it well without help, and the pilot teachers' time as coaches should be protected. Reporting to families is also framed as an obligation, since a short summary of what was tested, what happened and what the district decided shows that AI decisions are made carefully. The decisions themselves, about whether to widen, pause or stop a tool, remain with the school and district rather than with the tool or its vendor.
